specPoints.text: know that there is a force on a charged particle when it moves in a magnetic field as long as its motion is not parallel to the field

primer.text: A magnetic field picks on moving charges only — and even then only when they cut across the field lines. This note pins down the two conditions for the force, the perpendicular maximum, the parallel zero, and why a deflected beam changes direction without changing speed.

lessons.title: Forces on moving charges in magnetic fields
lessons.opening: A magnetic field grabs a charged particle only when it moves, and even then only when the motion has a component across the field lines. Parallel travel earns no force at all; perpendicular travel earns the maximum, which is why electron beams bend sideways — never forwards — as they cross a field.
keyPoints: A charged particle experiences a force in a magnetic field only while it is moving.
The force vanishes when the particle moves parallel to the magnetic field lines.
The force is greatest when the motion is perpendicular to the field lines.
The force direction depends on the sign of the charge, so electrons deflect opposite to positive charges.
The force acts at right angles to both the motion and the field, so it changes direction, not speed.

low.restatement: A still charge feels nothing in a magnetic field. Start it moving across the lines and it gets pushed sideways; move it along the lines instead and the push disappears.
low.analogy: Swimming across a river's flow drags you sideways, but floating straight along the current adds no sideways push.
low.examPointer: State both conditions in the mark scheme's order: moving AND not parallel to the field — dropping either loses the point.

medium.restatement: The magnetic force on a charge is the cross-product-style interaction: its magnitude scales with the charge, the speed, the field strength and the sine of the angle between velocity and field, so a parallel-travelling charge contributes zero through the sine term. Because the force is always perpendicular to the velocity, it does no work on the particle — it steers the path into an arc without changing the speed.
medium.analogy: A cue ball struck perfectly side-on changes direction but not pace: the sideways push redirects, it never accelerates the ball along its own line of travel.
medium.examPointer: For deflection questions, commit to the geometry: the beam curves across the field with a circular-style bend, and reversing the charge sign flips the bend to the other side.

check.stem: When does a charged particle feel a force in a magnetic field?

options.text: when it moves across the field lines instead of running along them
options.explanation: Both conditions — motion and a cross-field component — are required.

options.text: whenever it is inside the field, moving or not
options.explanation: A stationary charge feels no magnetic force.

options.text: only when it moves parallel to the field
options.explanation: Parallel motion is exactly the zero-force case.

options.text: only when the field is switched off
options.explanation: The force exists because of the field, not its absence.

check.stem: An electron travels along the magnetic field lines, never crossing them. What force does it feel?

options.text: zero
options.explanation: Motion parallel to the field produces no magnetic force.

options.text: maximum force along the field
options.explanation: Force acts across the field, and parallel motion cancels it entirely.

options.text: a sideways force into the page
options.explanation: No component across the field means no sideways push.

options.text: a force that slows the electron
options.explanation: The magnetic force never slows a charge to zero like this.

check.stem: The force on a moving charge in a magnetic field is greatest when the motion is:

options.text: perpendicular to the field lines
options.explanation: Perpendicular motion gives the full cross-field interaction.

options.text: parallel to the field lines
options.explanation: Parallel gives zero, the minimum not the maximum.

options.text: at 45 degrees to the field lines
options.explanation: 45 degrees gives a partial force, less than the perpendicular maximum.

options.text: opposite to the field direction
options.explanation: Anti-parallel is still parallel — zero force.

check.stem: A proton and an electron enter the same field with the same velocity, both moving across the field lines. How do their deflections compare?

options.text: they deflect towards opposite sides
options.explanation: The force direction follows the charge sign, so the two bend apart.

options.text: they deflect the same way
options.explanation: Opposite charges feel opposite force directions.

options.text: neither deflects
options.explanation: Cross-field motion gives both a force.

options.text: only the proton deflects
options.explanation: Both charged particles feel the field's force.

check.stem: What does the magnetic force do to the SPEED of a deflected electron?

options.text: the speed stays the same; only the direction changes
options.explanation: The force acts at right angles to the motion, steering without speeding.

options.text: the speed increases as it bends
options.explanation: A perpendicular force cannot push the particle faster along its path.

options.text: the speed decreases to zero
options.explanation: Nothing in the magnetic interaction stops the particle.

options.text: the speed first rises then falls
options.explanation: Speed is untouched throughout the deflection.

check.stem: State the two conditions needed for a charged particle to experience a force in a magnetic field.
check.modelAnswer: The particle must be moving, and its motion must not be parallel to the magnetic field lines.

check.stem: State the direction of the force on a moving charge relative to the field and the motion.
check.modelAnswer: The force is at right angles to both the velocity and the magnetic field lines.

check.stem: Explain why an electron moving exactly along a field line experiences no magnetic force.
check.modelAnswer: The magnetic force on a charge depends on the component of its motion across the field lines. Motion exactly parallel to the field has no cross-field component, so the field cannot exert any sideways push; the electron simply continues undeflected along the line.

check.stem: In a laboratory tube, a beam of electrons fires across a magnetic field at right angles. Describe and explain what an observer sees.
check.modelAnswer: The beam bends into a curve as it crosses the field, because each electron feels a force at right angles to its motion. The deflection is sideways — perpendicular to both the beam and the field — and reverses side if the field direction or the beam current is reversed.

glossary.definition: The push a magnetic field exerts on a moving charge crossing its field lines.
The sideways bending of a charged particle's path by a magnetic force.
The region around a magnet where magnetic forces act on moving charges.
